title: Data Masking
summary: Data masking replaces real sensitive values with realistic but false ones, so a copy of data can be used for testing, analytics or training without exposing the people in it. Static masking rewrites a copy in place, while dynamic masking changes values on the fly as a query returns them, leaving stored data untouched and usually driven by the requester's role. Effective masking preserves the properties the use case depends on, such as format, uniqueness and the referential links between tables, otherwise tests fail or joins break and teams quietly return to production data. The usual mistake is reversible obfuscation: encryption, unsalted hashing without a secret, or tokenisation that maps back to the original, all of which reduce to pseudonymisation and keep the same protection duties. Masking is not anonymisation unless re-identification is genuinely not reasonably possible.

beginner.definition: Data masking means replacing real sensitive values with fake but realistic ones. The copy can then be used for testing or analysis without showing private details. The fake data keeps the same shape, such as the length of a card number, so the systems still work.
beginner.whyItMatters: Test and training systems often hold copies of production data, and those copies are usually less protected. If real customer records sit in a test database, a small mistake there becomes a real breach. Masking lets teams work with useful data while the real people stay hidden. It also makes it easier to share data with partners under a contract. The risk of a costly leak drops when fake data is used instead.
howItWorks: The team lists the fields that hold personal or secret values, such as names and account numbers.
For each field they choose a method, such as shuffling, substituting or blanking values.
The masked copy is created from production data, usually on a fixed schedule.
Links between tables are preserved, so joins and reports still return sensible results.
Access rules decide who may see real values and who only sees the masked version.
The original data is removed from the test environment as soon as it is no longer needed.
beginner.example: Think of a training day for hospital staff. The trainees need to practise reading charts, but using real patient records would expose private details. So the trainers create charts for made up patients. The charts look real, with the same layout, the same kinds of notes and the same codes. A trainee can learn every step without ever seeing a real person's history. If the fake charts were random nonsense, the practice would teach nothing useful. That is why masked data must stay realistic. The fake patients must also never be traceable back to real people.
takeaways: Masked data must stay realistic, or tests and reports become useless.
Reversible masking is not the same as true anonymisation.
Remove the real data from test systems once a masked copy exists.

objectives: Explain what data masking is and why test data is a privacy risk.
Distinguish static masking from dynamic masking in a real environment.
Describe how format and referential integrity are preserved during masking.
Identify masking methods that remain reversible and explain the consequence.
Explain why masked data is not automatically anonymous data.
